The strangely sudden death r? Lord Digby, recalls Ito mind a strange incident in the career of his father. A.lmiral Sir Henry Dile*, which Lord Digby ' himself aced often to relate as absolutely true. It laid ti's, foundation of the family fortunes, and gained for the father of the peer just deceased the 009r11,1 by which he was forever afterwanis known I lin the navy•—that of the "Silver Captain." On 141 October. 1799, Admiral Sir Deury Dighy, then cap- tain commanding the frigate Alcmene, on n cruise ' oft: the Spanish coast, shaial his course for Cape St. Vincent, and wan running to the southward, in the latitude of Cape Finisterre. Twice in the night Sir , Henry rang his hell to aummon the officer of Hie , watch, and asked him if anybody had been in the 1 cabin. No, air; nobody." "Very odd," rejoined Dighy. "Every time I dropped ash•ep I heard somebody shouting in my tar, ' Dighy ! Dighy! go wto the noc liard ; Ingby ! Dighy ! go to the north- ward.' I shall certainly do so. div.head: NATIONAL LIBERAL CLUB.
div.p: NATIONAL LIBERAL CLUB.

Si, William Harcourt presided at a house dinner of the National Liberal Club on Wednesday evening held to celebrate the recent Liberal victontw. He said the Liberal party had no reason to be dissatisfital with their • position, they having won not only the seats which they lost in 1886, but also several whirl they did not hold in 1885. Ile predicted that the next genital election would exactly reverse the majority of the present Government. The recent elections would justify their leader in order- ing a general advance of the Liberal host, and giving the word of command, t• Up guards, and at them."

div.head: WELSH SUNDAY CLOSING ACT.
div.p: THE WELSH SUNDAY CLOSING ACT.

The sittings of the Royal Commission to iniquire into ! the Welsh Sunday Clesing Act, were nnomed at • jearmarthen, on Tues•lnny. The Chief C•nostable showed ;that the convictions for breach of the Act had increand ' since 1883. The effect of the Act was good in purely agricultural districts. In the mining districhn them wan latterly a lame increase of drunkenness. He believed • heavy peitaltitns would stop illicit sales. A petition from the townspeople in favour.of the Act was presented. On Thursday the Cemoissi.nn oat at Cardiff, anal the [witnesses suggented that sheboen keepers should bemore 1 strictly dealt with, and that publienhouses should be ; opened for a certain number of hours On Sunday.

div.head: ATHERTON MURDER.
div.p: THE ATHERTON MURDER.

PRISONER BEFORE THE LEIGH MAGISTRATES. i John Edward Lorne, who was appreheml of at Wigan on Friday night, on suspicion of being the non wantsi I Fir the Atherton murder, and who was before the Man- I Chester magistrates in Satunlay, who on Monday morns , ing placed lathe dock at Leigh Police Court chargiel with the murder of Walter Davies pawnbroker's ussistant, at Atherton on July 22. Mr. Fletcher proided, intl woo accompanied on the lieneh by :i somber of other ygstices : I The name of Lorne was at once callol. On entering the I dock he presented a very dissipattal appearance—Super- ' intendent Weir, who appeared for the police, said The prisoner Lorne, now before yoor Worships, is charged on suspicion with the murder of Walter Dames, on July 122. On that particular morning, Davies, who WWI I tent to John Lowe, pawnbroker,"Atherton, was murdered. ) Some time about nine o'clock the body; of Davies was found in the cellar of the monist's, and it saus subsequ- ently ascertained that a number of watches Did been stolen. In fact the deonsed's own watch and chain , were taken from his person. Since then the prisoner has , been taken into custody at Wigan,and handed overtone. I I don't propose to go on with the case toglay, but will ask for a remand imtil Wednesday. Last nights lawns broker's assistant came here frau Liverool and mid the prisoner was so like the man who had pawned one of the , stolen watches at their shop that he fully ',newel he was the man.—Superintendent Weir then went into the witness'bos, and in addition to his opening address, said that when the pawnbroker's assistant front Liverpog made his statement the prinmer in reply said, "I know nothing about it."—Mr. Fletcher Have you evidencg that the watch is the one stolen from the scene of the murder ? Supointendent Weir Oh yes, sir. I shall be able to idensify all the watches et:gen.—Mr. Fletcher (to 1 the prisoner) : Have you anything to my why you : should not lar remanded P—The prisoner: No.—Mr. Fletcher Then von stand remanded but Wednesday. Before the Leigh magistrates, on Wednesday morning, John Edward Lam, aged nineteen, was brought up on remand on stispicion of having murdered Walter Davies, a pawnbroker's assistant. at Atherton, on July 22nd., I Mr. Withers, of Blackburn, appeanal for the (Monier. Mr tilailat.aie Tee speech of Mr. I; tAIMiTONII at . at Southport will disappointtliose who have been expecting a new and great lin mouncement in the 410eStieeS of the day. Wt. were not. however, amongst those who anticipated a new departure: for in the first place that , w I Wil it is required. is the (motion ratherof the National Liberal Federation ; and in the second place no 11/11. keeWS better than the leader of the Liberal party that nothing can be done until the present litivernmsnt is replaced by a Government svh is prepared to grant Home Rule to Ireland. Tla. Tories seek to divert attention from their own weakness and mismanagement by demanding and re-demanding from Mr. GLAUSTONI: the ihetaib of 0110 w Home Rule measure. But clauses of bills are init usually drawn lip in public meeting.

. - Principles may be discussed and determined in that way ; lutil that is what has been done and is being done on the Irish question. The speech at South- port, on Wedneaday, was a review of the case against Coercion as it stands to-clay: and an exp,:sure4of the barrenness of 11,ivernment legisla- thm. Mr. DISRAELI once said that "Toryism is the elided ptirtica which engenders notl lill g " : and it inset be added that the cross with Liberal ism 41, awnot appearto renderthe animal mondruit-1 ftil.4ff the f. iiirteen measures promised in the Queen's ' iqweeb, eight, as MT. 11 LADSTON E 111ItS it, "have gone to the bottom .4 the sea: Of the six MOS- suns carried through, three were very "email beer,- and the other three " have hail the cordial support .4 the Liberal party." Mr. Gm mama s sounded a grave note lif warning with regard to Turkish misrule in Armenia inal in Crete. There is reason to fear that atrocities :ire being perpetra- tea similar to those which roused this country when Bulgaria was being held by the throat in 1870. There is denial of the charges so far as Turkey i ; concerned ; but eontnidiction Was proved to be sheer mendacity in 1870, and it may prove to be sheer mendacity in 1:::$9. It is the duty of Lord SALISBURY, as Prime Mininter, to do sonic- thing 111,0 than politely acknowledge these con- tradictions. Ile ought to inquire into the truth of the charges ; and, if he finds that they are well- founded, he might ti use the influent:A: of England in seeking to put cci end to the oppression of the Annenians. Mr. GLA DSTON E shows the wa.y,as he shows the way of getting rid 44 plirctioci in Ireland. Referring to the Unionist 'masts as to their succesa in gore g the sister country, the Liberal leader said, instead of removing restraints as they should have &ale as the result of their mem., " they had within the last few weeks been adding new lima:timed districts as tokens of their success in satisfying the aspirations of the Irish people." He paid a high tribute to Ireland for its imnmnity from crime, as apart from what was called agra- rian 4'rime; uml shattered the case of tire Govern- ment by imoting from official returns to the effect that agTSTi44II 0ff01144041 wen: 770 in Ifesfi as against 702 ill 14041, when according to the Tories. there was no neml for C,rercitrn. There is no need now ; it is all anomaly- it is 11Staill upon English govern- ment and it is the moral of Mr. GLADSTONE'S speech that Englishmen must wipe out this stain at the next election.
Tun large attendance at the Pnblie Warrington on Tuesday evening, and the ..•.

- . IfMt.. enthusiasm which was manifested, amply testify to the fact that Liberalism is alive in Warrington, and that all that is needed to en- sure success at the next election is good organise- that anal a good candidate. The proceedings were of more than average interest, for advantage was taken of the gathering to present Mr. JOHN Cans- mew, with a beautifully illuminated address, in recognitien of his countless services to the party. Mr. ( • els IMS isqi, associated all his life with the Liheradism of Warrington ; anal 111.1 IMEI always been as disinterested as he has outspoken in , whoa:Ming principles which have ever been dear to ! him. fle made a galiant, resolute light as the Liberal candidate at the last election ; but he fought under disadvantages common to the party: and it was semething achieved to have brought down the ;Averse majority from 776 to WI. It is a matter of gimeral regret that he could not see his' way to retaining the position of candidate; for we are sure lie spoke the language of conviction when he mitt he wan "perfectly madident that he could lick the Tories at the next election." He is obvi- ously in good fighting trim, and it i, it satisfaction to know that he will be ready, at the 'maker time, to struggle as hanl for another Liberal candidate as he would for himself. Alderman 111.1101,KM, who has for a generation been it commie in mins, made the prisontation in an appropri- ate speech ; and happily expres.stal the hope that he would live to see the day when one of Mr. Otosvistb's sons would represent Warrington in the House of Commons. The wish is, of course, father to the thought it is in that nature, tOO, of al pisithecy, and prophecies have sometimes a way if 11110111 g theIIISUIVOS. MT. WILMA M CROMFIKLM, : who 'castrated Warrington in I teci,when Liberalism ! was at its lowest ebb, was also present at the meeting ; and he was evidently touchml by the warmth of the reception which was accordetl He made a graceful and telling speech. MN mover of the resolution which expressed satisfaction at the iosults ci thw recent elections. and almost rivalled Mr. MeMi stows {lineal in illustrating his argnments with apt and hereon ais anecdote. Lin- coln will have a member of whom all classes may be proud when he is returned, as he will he returned, at the 'text general election.

This is the first time, we believe, belies addressed a Warrington audience ; lint it will not be the last, if the Liberals of the town can have their way, for it is not too much to say that he delighted all sections as much by his clearness and charm of I I style as by his fairness of statement, power of argument, and broad sympathy. Mr. ASQUITH understands every stop of the oratorical organ. It is an easy transition with him to pass "from grave to gay,froin livelv to severe.- He is etlective without straining after effect : and, better still, his manner earriev an assurance with it that he in striving not for an intellectual victory, hut for the advancement and the trimnpli of truth. Mr. 85L Louis has asked for argument, imil Mr. ASQUITH. in effect, says Be leisured thou shalt have ar;.,m- inent more than thou desirest." He traced the growth of the feel irg in favour of Home Rule, and frankly admitted that the Liberal party, profiting by the teachings of experience, hail left their old position and taken up a new one. The Tory party consented to move only when a convulsion Won spoil them ; and, putting the uliltiurorsee between the two in an epigrammatic form, Mr. ASQUITH said —" the progress of the Tory party is catastrophic, while the progress of the Lii,eral party is evolu- tionary." As bearing upon this point, it is of intermit to note that Mr. HERBERT GLAIWTONR, speaking at Peebles, on Saturday, quoted a letter written by Mr. lILAISITORK. in October, which, referring to local self-government, he said --" I do not on principle offer tiny limit to its ! exercise, except that the supremacy of the Imperial Legislature must for Imperial purposes he steadily maintained:* What, we would ask, is this but a statement, in brief, of the principle upon which Home Rule is hosed Further evidence that con- . version to Homo Rule was evolutionary in the mind of the great leader of the Liberal party is found in the fact that, before the elections of I seri, he intimated that, if Indandoinder the newly-acmiired franchise, made a distinct and practically unanimons demand it inight be necessary to make such changes as would go to the very root and foundation of the constitution. Mr. .ksuriru showed that he had a doe sense of the importance I.f this demand, whichi woo supported by four-fifths of the representatives of Ireland and he rated the Liberal Unionists, good-Immourmlly, for their disregard in this respect of Liberal principles. His speech was thnnighout as polished as it was argumentative ; and not the least important part of it was his remarks on the necessity, locally, of ihlfusing politi- cal education. The Libends have everything to , gain by discussion ; and there ought to lie several meetings in a year such as that held in the Public Hall on Tuesday. They would be a moans of sowing seed for a future harvest, and improve the prospect of Warrington at the next election.

Betting THE Rev. JOHN YONGE preached and an admirable sermon on betting am mg. and gambling, in Wycliffe Church, Warrington, on Sunday evening ; mol at the close of his discourse practical effect was given it by a number of pledges being taken to abstain from and discountenance these evil habits. It is to he hoped that the new " teetotal " movement will spread, for there can be no question as to the extension of the gambling mania during the! present generation. As Mr. YONG!: remarked, betting used to be the vice of the rich but it wlll5 now prevalent amongst all classes. The poor imitate the rich- -a fact which the rich ought ever to hear in mind loonier that they may be im- pressed with atoll sense of their responsibility to society. In this part of the country, betting upon horse racing has been largely promoted and stifnulated toy means of what are known as Connolly's Tickets: Hundreds of thousands of these tickets have been illegally sold ; and it has occasionally happened that a sabsidiary offender has been brought before the magistrates and heavily lined. But this was like diverting a tribu- tary rill, instead of stopping the stream at the fountain head; and we are glad to see that, no later than Monday last, the police of Liverpool entered find took possession of the premises where the tickets were being printed. "Connolly Tickets.' have been imfore the public for a quarter of a century ; and the mischief they have done in the meantime is incalculable. The plan in operation is in the nature a lottery on racing; and it is by means of these tickets that the young have been led on from what might seem an innocent transaction to betting on their OWO account. We are bound to say that the managers of church and chapel baraurs have thoughtlessly, (Jr recklessly, excited the gambling spirit by permitting raffles for the sale of goods. There OM be no question that it has often proved a ready way of raising the wind, and of getting rid of what inight have proved stir- phut stock. But it is one of those cases in which it cannot he said that the end justifies the means ; and it is satisfactory to observe how generally it , is being riamipiised that the custom is one which is more honoured in the breach than in the observance. Churchwardens and deacons who I have been party to trazaarrallt ,;cannot do better, as they have had to do with introducing the bane, than take stens to furnish the antidote. They will be well employed in following the Rev. John Yonge's example by making provision for obtain- ing plmlgee against betting and gambling. A word in time may prove to be all the difference in , a young life between that which mak.: and that ' which mars. Let the word lie simken.

A repr;e—n-tative meeting of railway servants Iva, held in the Victoria Inn, Sutton, on Saturday, for the purpose of considering tit., national programme of hours of railway servants as approves! at the con- gress held at hull on the lot inst. Mr. John Ren- ton, president of the St. Helens branch of the Amal- gamated Society of Railway Servants, occupied the chair, and said there was clearly a grievance among them. They were met to consider the national pro- gramme of hours of labour for railway servants, and he thought they were working under a great strain at present. After some discussion the following re- solution was passed "That OM meeting of railway servants approves of the national hours programme, and pledges itself to do all in its power to procure the same." acre.", and W. When Mr. Asquith 1.0(40 to respond to the vote of thanks at the Liberal meeting, on Tuesday, an ardent pol Annul exclaimed —" When are von coming again r The member for East Fife was ready with an answer, and instantly promised to mine again when they celebrated the return of a Liberal member for Warrington. We ean say " Amen to that : and the sooner the better—alike for the town and the country.

The " Spectat. ir." which went wrong with the Liberal Unionists, will not admit that approval of Home Ride is the cause of the recent Liberal vic- tories. It says --" Liberalism ;sac:Lilies, but Home Rule does not." Hy Liberalism is here meant the principles of Mr. Gladstone's followers ; and it is, to say the least of it, 1i singular admission. What will Mr. Chamberlain think of it He i would have the world believe that he carries the principles of Liberalism in his vest pocket, and he knows that they are not advancing.

The Tories are beginning to perceive that Free Education will make a solid plank in a platform audits they are hard up for a cry, it is not unlikely that they will seise on it. A London Correa - pondent, who is known to be a Conservative, declares that in Conservative circles the question is making" extraordinary headway." He goes on: --, I predict confidently," said one of the Govern- ment supporters sitting above the gangway, "that, if we do not get Free Education next year, we shall have it before a general election.

There can be no question that, if the Tories take op the cry of Free Education, it will, to a certain extent, serve them. But it is important to know how they will carry out the proposal. Are they going to tumble a large MIT into the laps of School Committees without exercising pro- per control over it Y Public money should be publicly spent by the representatives of the pub- lic, as is the case with Board SclusAs. It will he a fraud mans the taxpayers if education is to be made free at their expense and without their 0011 trol. "Taxation without representation is ty- ranny."

John L. Sullivan, the prize tighter, is a candi- date for a seat in the United States Legislature. He is going to plant himself, if becan, at Boston —Boston the home of culture, the hub of the !universe. John says—" A man, who can quieten a 11 crowd in Madison-square Gardens, as I have, can ' make has presence felt in Congress or anywhere else on earth." No doubt : if John took to hitting out, he would certainly make his presence felt. lie would hardly do as Chaplain to the House ; but he would make a capital chucker-out.

So the Rev. J. J. Longhorn will not leave the neighlmurhmol of Warrington after all. The liv- ing of Podgate, which is in the gift of the Rector of Warrington, has been °item' to the Clerical , Principal of the Clergy Daughters' School, and has been accepted by him. Thu Rector has made a wise choice, and he has, at the Nallie time, righted a wrong. We congratulate Mr. Langl insm the appointment ; and trust it will not prevent his retaining the post of honorary Secretory to the Warrington Temperance Federation.

The Federation commence a week's mission with I services to-morrow, followed by meetings in the !Public Hall every night next week. The mission ! is not before it is needed, for Warrington is a drink-ridden town. The Chief Constable described Buttermarket-st. so "unfit for a person to go up and down." He added that there were toiler twelve public-houses in this short street, and that it was inundated with people of questionalde character. A mission to the heathen ! And quite right, too, if we recognise that we have the heathen at our doors.

There was a lively scene at the Council meeting of the Alliance, on Tuesday. An attempt was made to slacken the reins by electing two gentle- men on the Committee of Forty who could not quite toe the prohibition mark. There was a strong feeling that this was to' advance two steps backward" ; hence the protest, and a round of voting which ended in the rejection of the gentle- men of uncertain sound. At present the policy c 4 the Alliance is a forward policy; the members feel that the next election will he their opportunity, and they mean to make the most of it.

'I A London Correspondent says :—A good story , used to be told of Mr. Disraeli about the time when on leaving Ake, he was scattering the usual golden shower of titles and rewards. THE FATALITY ON FRODSBAM SCORE.

„.._. The sum of £4O an. has been handed over by Mr. J. Weston, agent for the Weston section of the Ship Canal, to the parents of the unfortunate youth, Henry Sutton, !who was aceidentalle killed on the works of the Man- chester Ship Canal at Frodsham Score. on September 16th. £3O an. of this amount was collected Dom the employtlw on section Nn. 3, and and an additional £lO woo generously given by the contractor, Mr. T. A. Walker. SERIOUS ACCIDENT TO A LA!).

. ..... .......... . „ ... A youth named Armstrong Leigh. son if Peter Leigh, ' of Statham. Loam, was seriously injured ott the Statham section of the Ship Canal on Tureday. His btreiness was to move the points and so switch the train from one line to annther. He was in the act of doing so when a wagon laden with soil fell over on him. Active WlqiAtTflgte was at once renders!, and the youth retained to the hospital, when it woo found that his thigh was broken in three places. ACCIDENT ON THE SHIP CANAL AT THELWALL. An accident nf a somewhat unusual nature occurred on the Thelwall section of the Ship Canal, on Wednesday afternoon. Abont half-post five o'clock as a small locre motive with a train of trucks was parading in the diatitm of Acton Orange, it came into collision with • another engine to which wag attached a large number of heavily laden wagons, which was proceeding towards Salford. When a short distance from each other the drivers of the trains, seeing the danger to which they men' exposed and a possibility of collisions, intmediately shut off the steam, and reversed the engines, but caning to the wagons having such a heavy freight it wag impos- sible to prevent a collision. Both the locomotives were badly damaged, but the drivers and guards fortunately escaped injuo- by jumping lAT their respective engines. One of theta had a miraculous escape, :re he jumitni into the cutting beneath, a distanee of about 35 feet, but was • not hurt beyond a slight shaking. The damage is refills, • ted at abodt £l5O.

Sir,—May:Ttey. -;Oeir help follow up the swards I spoke last Sunday in nry own pipit at Wycliffe upon this I subject by a practical suggestion ? Convinced. I am of the imperative necessity of earnest 1 action against the further spread of these growing evils of the day. I desire to call the attention of all the Temperance and Rand of Hope Societies kettle town to work that they can well do in this direction. Let theft make no, of their ValiOUS meetings both for 1 adults and children to point on the miathievoves and evil . nature of hotting and gambling. Anil let them do noire than this. Could thsy not insert in their Temperance Pledges a spreitie clause against these practices ? My be- lief is t hat ifsaking thepledge is goshas a means of reform forsook as leave given way to drink, or as a preven. tire expedient whereby to train children to avoid the ese of drink, or, once more, if taking the pledge apainst drink is useful noon exampleto others to do so, then the same pause is likely to be goad against these pernicious habit of betting and gambling. I earnestly submit that this is a proper and desirable course to pursue. Si many instances have come °Mier my notice lately of the sorniw, and disgrace, and ruin produred in young men especially by- the practices alluded to, that I feel I cannot be silent or inactive in nispect of them. Surely everybody knows how terribly rife thew evils have become ! And seeing this to be the case, hit too much toasts that Christian people especially ahould cordially help any and every reasonable plan of remedy or of precaution? loin [...much even toast that they should cheerfully abandon nay little private and domestic indulgent:ins of their own, as yet perhaps of harmliss quantity, in these things, that by an example of abstinence from these practices they may make it easier tor young men and others to withstand tempts loon? The late John Bright said that it is in the power of Christian people to create a general public opinion in favour of Total Alstinence front the us of intoxicating drink." They are doing this more and more every year. , Let them go on to do so, more manifestly and con- spicuously still :and let them also take listW4-ork in hand. Th.e arc evils of the day, especially amangst young men, and they should be earnestly grappled with. I am glad to say that nearly 80 pledges against betting ! and gambling wen, taken after my sermon last Sunday evening, and I amthopeful to receive a large number in addition.—Yours faithfully, JOHN YONGE. Warrington, Oct 2301., 1880.

peaceful. and law-abiding citizen, will you be good enough to allow are to protest against what I considrr an abuse of" Religious Toleration." Unfortunately, I live next door to an individual whose house is the rendezvous, about three nights each week, for the members of a certain chapel choir. Now, sir, I am fond of music, and can fully appreciate a classical score well rendered, or even a decent sonata ; Nit when about half-a-dozen ancient hymn tunes are badly ren- dered, accompanied by the grinding of a harmonium about three-and-a-half notes flat. I beg to suggest Cuerd- ley Marsh or an old disused flat. When flattering invself of an evening on the absence of this torture, I ain disturbed nine times out of ten by other religious enthusiasts soliciting "subs." for the renovation of a church, the Society for Aid of Curates, Local Preachers' lb-nerve Fund, or !lOW other such charitable society which. rare on the occasion mentioned, one never hears of . . . . . . .

In hopes of evading such misery, last night I sauntered I ! down the town, towards the Library, ant encountered. I not fifty yards front the dn.... theSalyation Army in full !! blast. rhe music ! which floated from the adainantine throats of these prorm.inotrx was enough to make a coal 1! barge the. I flew wildly past these, happy in the pos. ' session of at least two hours' peace. But me. sir ;no ! peace for the wicked ; the churelt bells next pealed forth their wretched beadssplitting ding-dong the whole of the I conevening.tend, Mr. Editor. that no religious party has I a right to interfere with the egFinfort and quietness of ratepayers who are in the minority, however small that minority may happen to be. If a churchman has the ; right to prevent any night's study, and replace it with , • headache, surely a Mormon or Maltommedan has a right to take unto himself two wives, or more, if he can decently keep them. Many of the rites of Brahmins, Buddhists. or even heathens objected to by Christians, , would be leas public nuimnces than many we are sub- , jected to under the garb of Christianity. To crown all, after being humbuggeil on every side all . week by religionists, lain prevented on Sunday from investing an honest penny, quietly and unobtrusively, on a" Sunday Chroniele:"fhanking you in anticipa- tion, I am. coats truly, " DO UNTO OTHERS AS OTHERS DO YOU."
